NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday described India’s youth as the country’s biggest strength, but said a lack of jobs, expensive education, paper leaks, poor access to credit and the growing use of AI were holding them back.Speaking at the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ programme at KP Ground in Prayagraj, Rahul told the gathering, “You are power and pride of India; when I say this, I talk about every Indian citizen.” He said he wanted to speak about “dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)”, framing his address around the problems facing young Indians and the economic resources he believes should belong to them.Rahul said India’s nearly 40 crore young people were its “greatest strength”, adding that while there was much discussion about America, China and Russia, “India’s youth [are] unparalleled.” He argued that the country's future would depend on the potential of its young population and the data they generate.He said artificial intelligence was also built on people’s data and argued that this data should be treated as an asset belonging to Indians. Rahul criticised the growing use of AI in discussions about employment, saying technological changes could further threaten jobs unless young people benefited from the economy being built around their data.Rahul also spoke about his connection to Prayagraj, describing the city as his family’s home and recalling its past as an important educational centre. He said Allahabad University had once been among the country's best universities.Rahul said young Indians were being trapped in a “chakravyuh”, with education becoming increasingly expensive while degrees often failed to translate into jobs.“Today, education certificates have no meaning in India because they cannot give you job,” he said, arguing that students could spend years and large amounts of money on education without finding meaningful employment.Rahul said the problems extended across several routes into the workforce. “All doors of employment are closed in India,” he said, pointing to a decline in manufacturing, difficulties in securing loans, government-exam paper leaks and AI-driven job losses.“Decline in manufacturing, hard-to-come-by loans, paper leaks, AI replacing jobs – all this is hurting India's youth,” Rahul said.He blamed demonetisation and GST for hurting small industries, alleged that banks were failing to provide adequate credit to small and medium businesses, and criticised the privatisation of public-sector companies. He also argued that AI could further reduce corporate employment while young Indians were increasingly pushed towards gig work.Rahul framed these problems as part of what he called the broader “system”, arguing that economic and political power had become concentrated among a small number of people. He linked this to his criticism of large corporations, the government and the RSS, alleging that they exercised disproportionate influence over India's institutions.Rahul said recent student protests showed that young Indians were beginning to challenge the system. “Youths lit a light in darkness, and in doing so, changed the country,” he said.He urged young people to confront their fears without resorting to hatred or violence. “You cannot hate or be violent,” Rahul said, adding, “We will never resort to hatred or violence; will change the system with love and affection.”
Article Summary: Rahul Gandhi spoke at the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme at KP Ground in Prayagraj. He said he wanted to speak about ‘dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)’ He argued that the country's future would depend on its young population.

Article Title: Bihar should withdraw alcohol ban as it failed to curb crimes against women: Report
Article Text:
Representative image

Ban failed to reduce crimes against women, says paper

Prohibition has also hit state revenues

Education, health and jobs among Bihar's priorities

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Bihar should withdraw its prohibition on alcohol as the ban has failed to reduce crimes against women and has been accompanied by a rise in illicit liquor and alternative intoxicants, according to a research paper by economic think tank National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).The paper, titled ‘Macro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forward’, also said restoring liquor excise duty to pre-ban levels could increase the state's own revenues by 14-15 per cent while reducing expenditure on enforcement and anti-smuggling operations.Prepared by a team of economists led by Ratna Sahay and presented at the India Policy Forum, the paper examined the economic and social impact of Bihar's prohibition, introduced in April 2016.The paper said the primary reasons for introducing prohibition were the belief that alcohol consumption contributed significantly to domestic violence and that households would redirect money previously spent on alcohol towards more productive uses.Women's groups and activists had also strongly backed the ban, arguing that prohibition would reduce alcohol-related abuse.However, the NCAER researchers said available data now allows an assessment of whether those objectives were achieved.“We now have sufficient data and information to assess if the ban was effective. Reported crimes against women in Bihar have not declined following the introduction of prohibition. Instead, total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period,” the paper said.According to the study, the available evidence does not show a broad-based reduction in crimes against women after prohibition. Instead, it said the ban coincided with concerns over the expansion of illicit liquor networks, enforcement difficulties and corruption.The paper also pointed to increased use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs.“In tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs,” it said.The NCAER paper said Bihar suffered significant fiscal consequences after the ban. Before prohibition, excise duty on alcohol accounted for about 14 per cent of the state's own revenues in the three years preceding the ban.At the same time, the government incurred higher expenditure on monitoring, enforcement and anti-smuggling operations, which the paper said added to fiscal pressures.The researchers argued that reinstating liquor excise duty at historical levels could help restore the contribution of the tax to around 14 per cent of state revenues.The paper concluded that the prohibition had not achieved its intended objectives and had instead coincided with higher reported crimes against women, loss of state revenue and increased enforcement expenditure.Beyond prohibition, the paper identified six interconnected areas that it said should form the core of Bihar's development strategy: education, health, governance and law and order, flood mitigation, private-sector development and women's empowerment.It said reforms in these areas were necessary to improve productivity, accelerate structural transformation and create better-quality jobs for Bihar's young population.The study also examined the state's public debt and fiscal sustainability, and assessed the financing required for different reform scenarios. It called for a combination of stronger own-revenue mobilisation, more efficient public spending, additional central government support and, where necessary, further borrowing.The paper noted that improvements in law and order had played an important role in Bihar's economic recovery after 2005, when the state government under Nitish Kumar placed greater emphasis on policing, criminal prosecution, judicial reforms and administrative accountability.It also highlighted Bihar's significance for India's broader development goals, noting that the state is the country's second most populous and remains its poorest.Bihar's population is estimated at 13.2 crore in 2026, according to the paper, accounting for more than 9 per cent of India's population. It noted that the state's population is larger than that of all but 10 sovereign countries.
Article Summary: Ban failed to reduce crimes against women, says paper by economic think tank NCAER. Prohibition has also hit state revenues, according to the research paper. Education, health and jobs among Bihar's priorities, says the paper. It also highlighted Bihar's significance for India's broader development goals.

Article Title: Safety vs privacy: How domestic-help platforms are building a two-way support system
Article Text:
A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprise of women.

Formalising trust in an informal workforce

Safety vs surveillance divide

Safety by design

What women check before opening the door

The rituals of being home alone

The older customer’s definition of trust

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The next phase of trust

India’s instant domestic help economy is expanding faster. App-based platforms promise cleaners, cooks and household workers within minutes. However, the real contest here is no longer just about speed, convenience or pricing. It is increasingly about trust.A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprises women.For years, domestic work in India has operated through informal neighbourhood networks, word-of-mouth referrals and personal recommendations. The new generation of platforms is attempting to formalise that ecosystem by adding identity verification, digital payments, ratings, training, insurance and customer support.But unlike food delivery or ride-hailing, these services involve something far more intimate: a stranger entering a private home.That has forced platforms to solve an unusually difficult problem. They must simultaneously protect women who enter unfamiliar homes for work and women who may be home alone when they invite those workers inside.The result is a rapidly evolving safety architecture built around background checks, restricted service hours, real-time monitoring, SOS systems, human escalation teams and, increasingly, AI-assisted risk detection.India’s domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base.But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.A spokesperson for Pronto shared the measures it takes to ensure transparency, saying that every worker completes criminal court record verification and police verification before joining the platform. Customers, too, verify their name, phone number and address through OTP authentication and must agree to a code of conduct before placing a booking.Pronto's workers, for example, receive training before taking their first assignment, and that low customer ratings are investigated by trainers rather than triggering automatic deactivation.“Every hub we operate doubles as a training centre, and a professional takes her first booking only after she is trained, background-verified and dispatch-ready, a process that takes about four days,” the spokesperson said.Similarly, Snabbit, whose workforce consists entirely of women professionals, said it has built a multi-layered safety framework supported by a dedicated Trust & Safety team.A spokesperson said the system includes “mandatory KYC and background checks for all experts on the platform, verified customers, address-level traceability and controlled job allocation.”The sharpest divide between platforms and customers is emerging around body-worn cameras.Pronto has begun experimenting with optional recorded bookings designed to protect workers from false allegations in cases of disputes with customers.For many users, however, the presence of a camera inside a private home changes the nature of the interaction. “I know some platforms are starting to equip their workers with chest-mounted bodycams for transparency, and while I understand it protects the worker from false claims, it completely freaks me out as a customer,” a Delhi resident said.“My home is my private sanctuary. The idea of a stranger walking through my living room with an active lens, recording the exact layout of my home, my entrances, my exits, my personal belongings, and where my work setup or valuables are, feels like an extreme invasion of privacy.”Her concerns extend beyond the recording itself. “Where is that video footage stored? Who at the tech company has access to it? Could that footage leak or be hacked?” she said. “I would honestly think twice before booking a service that mandates live video recording inside my private space. There has to be a boundary between physical safety and digital surveillance.”Pronto, however, ensured that the sole mechanism of this process is to ensure safety and privacy.It said that additional video data is collected only on opt-in verified bookings. According to its spokesperson, customers choose the feature during booking and confirm it again when the worker arrives. The camera is tilted downward to capture only the work area, records no audio, blurs faces and personal information on the device itself, deletes raw footage immediately, and retains only an anonymised encrypted version for a limited review period and AI training.One of the most striking trends across the sector is that many safety measures are designed not around responding to incidents, but around preventing high-risk situations from arising in the first place.Several platforms have restricted service hours, particularly avoiding late-evening and night bookings when women workers may be required to enter unfamiliar homes after dark.Snabbit said its safety system monitors active jobs in real time and can identify anomalies that may require intervention. According to its spokesperson, “Active jobs are monitored in real time, with the dedicated Trust & Safety team supporting rapid escalation and incident response.”For many women, however, trust begins long before a worker arrives.A 24-year-old student in Jaipur said she has developed a consistent checklist before booking any on-demand domestic service. She checks whether the app displays a verified profile with a photograph, ID verification, ratings and reviews, and prefers platforms that offer real-time tracking and OTP-based service verification.“The first thing I check is whether the app shows a verified profile with a photo, ID verification, ratings, and reviews from other women,” she said. “Real-time tracking and an OTP-based start and end of the service also make me feel more comfortable.”Before the worker arrives, she follows a set of precautions that have become almost automatic. She keeps her phone fully charged, informs at least one friend that someone is coming over, avoids leaving valuables or personal documents in plain sight, and stays in a part of the house where she can easily monitor what is happening.“I usually make sure my phone is fully charged and I let at least one friend know that someone is coming over,” she said. “If it’s a longer service, I stay in a part of the house where I can easily see what’s happening.”She is also careful about digital privacy. “I prefer apps that mask phone numbers, and I never share extra details unless they’re necessary for the service,” she said. “I avoid mentioning that I live alone or discussing my schedule. Once the job is done, I’m careful not to continue communication outside the platform.”For her, safety is not just about preventing a crime; it is about minimising information that could make her vulnerable later.Minal, a 26-year-old professional in Delhi described a different set of habits that have emerged through repeated use of instant service platforms. While the agent is at home, she stays in the hall rather than a closed bedroom, keeps her phone in her hand, and deliberately leaves a pair of her partner’s or male flatmate’s shoes near the entrance.“I never sit in my bedroom with the door shut. I stay in the main living area, usually at the dining table with my laptop,” she said. “I also leave a pair of my male flatmate’s or partner’s shoes near the entryway. It’s a small mental trick, but it makes me feel less exposed.”She and two close friends have an informal safety protocol built around messaging apps.“I have a private WhatsApp group with two close friends. We have a tacit rule: whenever an instant maid or repair person is assigned, I drop the tracking link, their name, and a quick ‘Expected time: 45 mins,’” she said. “I don’t overthink it, but it gives me a safety net.”When asked what app features actually make her feel secure, she was sceptical of marketing labels.“Honestly, badges and ‘police verified’ tags on an app screen don’t mean much to me anymore. Anyone can upload a document,” she said. “What actually makes me feel safe is seeing a real-time, live selfie of the person taken right when they accept the job, matching the photo on their profile. Plus, knowing there’s a strict OTP entry system where they can’t start billing until I give them a code at the door.”Her distinction is important: she is less interested in historical verification and more interested in real-time authentication.For older users, digital verification often feels less persuasive than physical verification. Sarita , a 52-year-old homemaker in Delhi-NCR, said she places greater trust in tangible indicators such as uniforms, identity cards and residential security systems.“A professional now gets to share her version of events and any relevant information before a decision is taken, and we work to keep investigations balanced and transparent,” Pronto spokesperson said.That shift, from treating workers merely as service providers to treating them as rights-bearing participants in the platform ecosystem, may prove as important as any technological innovation.As instant domestic help services expand beyond metropolitan cities into smaller urban centres, safety may become the industry’s primary competitive differentiator.Speed is easy to advertise. Trust is harder to build.Women are asking for features that combine digital verification with human accountability: live identity confirmation, female-worker filters, trusted-contact notifications, residential gate integration, discreet exit mechanisms, neighbourhood-level reputation and transparent data governance.Platforms, meanwhile, are investing in training hubs, background verification, restricted service hours, SOS networks, counselling, insurance and AI-assisted monitoring.
Article Summary: India’s domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base. But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.

NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has suspended the licences of two food manufacturers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra after inspections uncovered serious food safety violations, including live insects in pistachios, rodent droppings, fungal growth, unhygienic processing conditions and ineffective pest control.The action was taken against VKC Nuts Private Limited (Uttar Pradesh) and Chheda Specialities Foods Pvt Ltd (Maharashtra), with FSSAI saying the deficiencies posed a potential risk to public health.At VKC Nuts, inspectors found live insects in stored pistachios, heavy black mould on storage walls and ceilings, rodent droppings across the premises, rusted machinery, damaged flooring, houseflies on food products and a live lizard near open crates of figs. Article Title: Supriya Sule opposes FCRA Bill, urges Centre to withdraw it or send it to JPC
Article Text:
Supriya Sule said foreign funding should not automatically be treated with suspicion

‘ Foreign funding cannot always be viewed with suspicion’

Sule backs youth protests, questions party symbol decisions

NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) working president Supriya Sule on Saturday opposed the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 in its present form, urging the Centre either to withdraw the proposed legislation or refer it to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for wider discussion.Sule, the Lok Sabha MP from Baramati, said all political parties should be given an opportunity to examine the contentious legislation before Parliament takes it up for consideration. She cautioned the government against rushing the bill through Parliament, amid reports that it could be discussed and passed next week.“We reject and disagree with the present form of the FCRA bill. If the government is not ready to withdraw the bill, then it should send it to a JPC. In a strong democracy, merely opposing something is not enough; we also have to sit together and discuss it,” she said.The proposed legislation seeks to establish a designated authority for the vesting, supervision, management and disposal of foreign contributions and assets in cases involving cancellation, surrender or expiry of an organisation’s FCRA registration.The bill also provides for provisional and permanent vesting of such assets.Critics have argued that the proposed changes could give the government greater control over organisations receiving foreign contributions.Sule said foreign funding should not automatically be treated with suspicion, arguing that overseas contributions can support legitimate work in areas such as healthcare and education.She said action should be taken if foreign funds are linked to illegal activities such as drug trafficking or terrorism, but questioned the rationale for viewing every foreign-funded organisation negatively.“There are organisations such as the Gates Foundation and USAID that have been doing good work for many years. Why should we look at every foreign-funded organisation with a bad eye?” she said.She also compared foreign funding with money sent home by Indians living abroad, arguing that the source of money alone should not determine whether it is viewed negatively.According to official figures, 13,520 entities received foreign remittances totalling Rs 55,741 crore between 2019 and 2022.As of July 15, 2026, there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations, while 22,498 registrations had been cancelled and 15,212 had expired.The FCRA regulates the receipt and utilisation of foreign contributions by NGOs, charitable institutions, educational bodies, religious trusts and other organisations.Sule also commented on the ongoing protests by students, saying young people should not face such treatment while seeking education.“What happened at Jantar Mantar should not happen anywhere in the country. Our children want to study and this is happening to them. I read that ministers from Jharkhand have ordered an inquiry into it,” she said.She also backed Uddhav Thackeray in the dispute over the Shiv Sena's name and election symbol, arguing that party organisations and constitutions should be considered while deciding control of political parties.On the NCP dispute, Sule said the legal battle remained unresolved and alleged that her party had been waiting for a hearing.“Sharad Pawar is the founder president of the NCP and injustice has been done to him. We have been asking for a date for a long time, but why are we not getting a date?” she said.Sule also criticised the Maharashtra government's approach to farm loan waivers and called for political criticism to remain focused on issues rather than becoming personal.On the proposed delimitation legislation, Sule said it would be premature to comment before the bill was introduced. She added that the NCP (SP) would discuss the legislation with its alliance partners once it came before Parliament.Sule further said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had agreed to meet NCP (SP) MPs on Monday to discuss issues concerning their constituencies, amid the opposition's contention that Parliament was not functioning properly.
Article Summary: Supriya Sule opposes the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 in its present form. She urged the Centre either to withdraw the proposed legislation or refer it to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for wider discussion. Sule said foreign funding should not automatically be treated with suspicion.

Article Title: India to recover 'Green Boots' climber's body from Everest after 30 years: Report
Article Text:
"Green Boots," the climber India is bringing home. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

The climber behind the ‘ Green Boots ’ mystery

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The body of an Indian climber believed to have become the mountaineering world’s infamous “Green Boots” could finally be brought down from Mount Everest, three decades after he died while descending from the summit.India is preparing a high-altitude recovery mission to retrieve the remains of Dorje Morup, an Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) personnel who died on Mount Everest in 1996, according to a detailed report by the BBC.Morup’s body has remained frozen at about 8,500 metres on the northern side of Everest for nearly 30 years. The remains became known among climbers as “Green Boots” because of the distinctive bright green mountaineering boots visible on the body.The ITBP is now looking for a specialist team capable of undertaking the difficult recovery operation. The force hopes to bring the remains back to India by September, after which DNA testing would be carried out to establish Morup’s identity conclusively, the BBC reported.If the identification is confirmed, his remains will be returned to his family in Ladakh.Morup was 48 when he joined a six-member ITBP expedition that attempted to climb Everest from the Chinese side in 1996.The expedition was seeking to become the first Indian team to reach the summit from that route.Three members of the expedition eventually turned back because of a snowstorm, while Morup and fellow climbers Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor continued towards the summit.All three reached the top, but disaster struck as they attempted to descend.A blizzard hit the mountain and killed the three climbers. Their bodies were left on Everest, as recovering bodies from the mountain is itself an extremely dangerous undertaking.For years, the body now known as “Green Boots” was assumed to belong to Paljor. However, surviving members of the 1996 expedition, along with information about the climbers’ final radio communications and the location of the body, have led authorities to believe that it was actually Morup.An ITBP official told BBC that Morup’s clothing and climbing equipment had also helped authorities identify the remains in recent years.The body has since become one of the most recognisable markers on the route to Everest’s summit, passed by climbers making their way through the mountain’s notorious “death zone”.For Morup’s family in Ladakh, the operation could finally resolve a mystery that has lasted three decades.His wife, Konchak Yangskit, told the BBC that she struggled to accept his death because she had never seen his body.Morup had told her before leaving for the expedition that he would return home after making the country proud. He had also asked her to look after their children and come to the airport to receive him when he returned.His son, Punchok Dorjai, told the BBC that the family plans to hold a funeral near Martyrs Park in Leh if the remains are confirmed as his.He also said the family intends to keep the green boots that gave Morup's remains their enduring identity on Everest.
Article Summary: Dorje Morup died on Mount Everest in 1996. His body has remained frozen at about 8,500 metres on the northern side of Everest for nearly 30 years. The remains became known among climbers as ‘Green Boots’ because of the distinctive bright green mountaineering boots visible on the body.

A delegation of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) arrived in Ranchi on Saturday to extend support to students protesting alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC).CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said the party stood in “complete solidarity” with the protesting students and would provide them with all forms of support.“CJP stands in complete solidarity with the students of Jharkhand,” Ranka said in a post on X.He added that the delegation was travelling under the leadership of Mukallrounder and Akshay Shinde and would support the students during their ongoing agitation.Speaking to PTI, CJP national coordinator Mukesh said the party fully supports students protesting over alleged irregularities in JPSC and JSSC examinations and repeated paper leaks. “We stand with the students and will continue to support them,” he said, adding that the party would share its experience from the Jantar Mantar movement with the protesting students.“Our support may not be from the stage, but we are standing with them,” Mukesh said, asserting that the CJP would continue backing the students until there is transparency in recruitment examinations and paper leaks are stopped.“Till when will this continue to happen?” he asked.The protests in Jharkhand have intensified following allegations of irregularities in recruitment examinations. Article Title: 'Which freedom fighter received most severe punishment?' Kerala orders probe into Savarkar quiz
Article Text:
File photo: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar

Education department says quiz was not authorised

Pinarayi Vijayan accuses government of 'colluding' with RSS

Left groups, IUML leaders criticise question

NEW DELHI: A political row has erupted in Kerala over a school quiz question that described Hindutva ideologue Vinayak Damodar Savarkar as the freedom fighter who received the "most severe punishment" from the British, prompting general education minister N Samsudheen to order an inquiry.The "Freedom Quiz" was conducted on August 6 for lower primary students in schools in the Kasaragod, Kumbla and Manjeshwar sub-districts, according to news agency PTI.The disputed question asked: "Who is the freedom fighter that received the most severe punishment from the British?" Savarkar was given as the answer.The minister's office said Samsudheen has directed the director of general education to establish who prepared and conducted the quiz and take stringent action against those responsible.According to the minister's office, the quiz was not included in the activity calendar of either the Social Science Club or the General Education Department. Neither had authorised anyone to independently prepare the questions or conduct the competition."The person who included the historically incorrect question holds a prejudiced view," the minister's office said, adding that the Education Director had been instructed to identify those responsible and take strict action.As per PTI, teachers associated with the Social Science Club had prepared the questionnaire.The controversy has since drawn criticism from the CPI(M) and Left-affiliated student and youth organisations, which accused the Congress-led UDF government of allowing what they described as a "Sangh Parivar agenda" to enter the education system.CPI(M) veteran and former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan accused the UDF government of "colluding" with the RSS and alleged that efforts were being made to conceal Savarkar's history and glorify him.Addressing a press conference in Kannur, Vijayan alleged that the Centre and the RSS were attempting to "rewrite history". He also linked the controversy to the Centre's efforts to implement its new education policy in Kerala.Former general education minister V Sivankutty also criticised the question, alleging that it was part of an attempt to "saffronise" Kerala's general education sector and distort the history of India's freedom struggle.Sivankutty demanded a comprehensive inquiry, strict action against those responsible and the withdrawal of the disputed question and answer. He also sought an apology from the General Education Department.SFI state secretary P S Sanjeev alleged that the quiz sought to portray Savarkar as a freedom fighter. In a social media post, he criticised the UDF government and alleged that the general education portfolio was being used to create space for the Sangh Parivar.DYFI state secretary K Sanoj also criticised the government, saying there was no justification for a school quiz to contain a question that allegedly glorified Savarkar.Senior Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) leader and former minister M K Muneer said portraying Savarkar as a patriot was part of the RSS-BJP agenda.Muneer, however, said that if the question had indeed been included in the quiz, the matter should be seriously examined and those responsible identified, adding that it should not be treated lightly.
Article Summary: "Freedom Quiz" conducted on August 6 for lower primary students in schools in Kasaragod, Kumbla and Manjeshwar sub-districts. Question asked: "Who is the freedom fighter that received the most severe punishment from the British?" Savarkar was given as the answer. Education department says quiz was not authorised.

Article Title: 'Army safeguarding territory': Arunachal CM Pema Khandu rejects Chinese encroachment
Article Text:
Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu

NEW DELHI: Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu on Saturday rejected reports of Chinese military encroachment in the state and said that the Army was effectively patrolling and safeguarding the territory.Speaking to reporters, Khandu said, "No signs of encroachment in Arunachal Pradesh; Indian Army effectively patrolling and safeguarding the territory."Khandu's remarks came a day after the Centre identified 27 locations in Arunachal Pradesh by their standard names on the official map of the country, amid China's repeated attempts to rename places in the border state.The government said the exercise was aimed at ensuring the correct identification of the locations and improving public awareness of their geographical and historical significance."Identifying them formally on the Survey of India map of Arunachal Pradesh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large," an official statement said.New Delhi has consistently rejected Beijing's practice of assigning Chinese names to places in Arunachal Pradesh, calling the move "vain and preposterous".India has maintained that such actions do not alter the "undeniable" fact that Arunachal Pradesh "was, is, and will" remain an integral part of the country.Several of the locations newly marked on the official map hold strategic importance because of their proximity to the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and their role in past India-China military confrontations.Among them is Long Ju, one of the earliest flashpoints between the two countries. Chinese troops entered the area in 1959, three years before the 1962 India-China war.The official map also includes Maja village in Upper Subansiri district near Long Ju, Bisa village and the strategically significant mountain passes of Dzo La, Riza La and Pukur La.Another key location is Thag La, the high-altitude pass where one of the opening battles of the 1962 India-China war took place.Jairampur in Changlang district has also been formally identified. The town serves as an important logistics hub for the movement of security forces towards eastern Arunachal Pradesh and the Myanmar border.Other locations added to the map include the high-altitude lake Sambho Sarovar, Bara Kundun, Chhota Kundun, Dhan Bari, Pritnagar, Teritnagar, Ramnagar, Jaswant Garh, Sagar, Padma, Jyotinagar, Baisakhi, Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, Chhota Ropuk, Bara Ropuk, Shivaji Nagar, Sunpura, Kamlang Nagar and Buddhamandir.India has repeatedly dismissed China's attempts to assign what it calls "fictitious names" to places in Arunachal Pradesh, saying such efforts seek to create "baseless narratives" and cannot alter the "undeniable" reality on the ground. New Delhi has also warned that such actions could undermine efforts to improve bilateral ties.China first issued a list of six standardised names for places in what it calls Zangnan in 2017. It followed this with a second list covering 15 locations in 2021 and another naming 11 places in 2023. Beijing uses the term Zangnan to refer to Arunachal Pradesh, a claim India has consistently rejected.
Article Summary: Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu rejects reports of Chinese military encroachment in the state. He said that the Army was effectively patrolling and safeguarding the territory. His remarks came a day after the Centre identified 27 locations by their standard names on the official map.

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal on Saturday backed the immediate implementation of the Constitution Amendment Bill, providing for women's reservation, along with "fair and equitable" delimitation, a day after party president Sukhbir Singh Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi.In a post on X, Badal said the party draws inspiration from the Sikh Gurus, who championed the dignity, equality and equal rights of women."The Shiromani Akali Dal, at a meeting of its senior leaders in Chandigarh today, demanded the immediate implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill in the country. The Shiromani Akali Dal draws inspiration from the teachings of the Sikh Gurus, who championed the dignity, equality and equal rights of women. The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee has already set an example by providing for women's reservation in its House," Badal said."After detailed deliberations on key issues before Parliament, the Shiromani Akali Dal also demanded a fair and equitable delimitation that ensures equal representation to all states. The Shiromani Akali Dal supported the proposal put forward by the Government of India on the floor of the House for a uniform 50 percent increase in the number of seats for all states.The party emphasised that women's reservation and delimitation should be implemented immediately," he added.The development comes amid speculation that Badal's meeting with PM Modi could pave the way for the erstwhile allies to join hands again ahead of the Punjab assembly elections due early next year.The Akali Dal left the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over differences surrounding the Centre's three farm laws, which were repealed in 2021.Once Punjab's dominant political combine, the BJP and SAD have spent the past several years on the margins of state politics, watching their traditional support base erode as the Kejriwal-led Aam Aadmi Party emerged as the state's principal political force.Even after the Narendra Modi government repealed the laws in 2021, ties between the former allies remained strained.In the 2022 Punjab assembly elections, voters rejected both the Congress and the former allies, delivering a sweeping mandate to the Aam Aadmi Party.When asked about the possibility of the two parties stitching an alliance again, the state BJP chief said he could not say anything about it.Senior SAD leader and party spokesperson Daljit Singh Cheema, when asked about what transpired at the meeting, told PTI, "I can only say that the two leaders have met."Senior party leader Sikandar Singh Maluka told PTI that the current situation in Punjab demands a SAD-BJP alliance. He, however, clarified that it was his personal opinion and not that of the party."If an alliance is to be stitched, what will be the conditions? Any decision on this will be taken after due deliberations in the party," Maluka said, adding, "The sentiment of people is that SAD and BJP should form an alliance. This is not the party's opinion but my own."
Article Summary: Shiromani Akali Dal backs immediate implementation of the Constitution Amendment Bill, providing for women's reservation. Party president Sukhbir Singh Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Badal said the party draws inspiration from the Sikh Gurus, who championed the dignity, equality and equal rights of women.

Article Title: IT ministry asks Meta to revamp algorithms, submit roadmap to tackle deepfakes
Article Text:

Meta outlines technical measures

Meta under growing government scrutiny over CSAM

NEW DELHI: The ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) has asked Meta to revamp its algorithms and submit a compliance roadmap aimed at curbing deepfakes, propaganda and other manipulated or illegal content on its platforms.The directive was issued during recent discussions between MeitY officials and Meta, amid growing concerns over the spread of synthetic and manipulated content online, ANI cites.Officials have asked the social media giant to strengthen its content moderation systems and act faster on takedown requests from authorised government agencies, the sources said.MeitY also sought greater compliance with data-localisation requirements and asked Meta to work more closely with government agencies to speed up the identification and removal of deepfakes, morphed images and misleading posts.The government has also pushed for specific algorithmic changes to limit the reach and amplification of propaganda and manipulated media.The directive followed talks in which Meta acknowledged gaps in its existing systems and outlined technical measures it could take to address deepfakes and other synthetic content, the sources said.During a meeting with MeitY officials on Friday, Meta's technical team explained how the company currently detects and handles harmful content on its platforms.Officials, however, pressed for more concrete changes to the algorithms governing the spread of such content and sought a clear compliance roadmap from the company.Both sides agreed to continue discussions on the issue, with another meeting expected next week, ANI reports.The government's scrutiny of Meta has intensified in recent days over concerns surrounding deepfakes, Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) and other harmful content on its platforms. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had earlier apologised over errors related to CSAM and deepfake content after concerns were raised by the Indian government.The latest discussions come as India has tightened its regulatory framework for synthetically generated content, including through amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules earlier this year. The revised rules introduce additional due-diligence requirements for online intermediaries and seek greater accountability for AI-generated and manipulated content.
Article Summary: The directive was issued during recent discussions between MeitY officials and Meta, amid growing concerns over the spread of synthetic and manipulated content online. Officials have asked the social media giant to strengthen its content moderation systems and act faster on takedown requests from authorised government agencies.
